why_use_this: Reach for this package for the two classical, well-understood ML tasks (linear/logistic regression, k-means clustering) plus the supporting data-pipeline utilities (scaling, train/test/k-fold splitting, one-hot encoding, metrics) any ML workflow needs around the model itself -- built as thin, tested wrappers over [vani-probability](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-probability)'s regression and [vani-optimize](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-optimize)'s gradient descent rather than reimplementing them. For anything beyond classical ML -- a small neural network, a custom loss you need the gradient of automatically rather than hand-deriving -- this package ALSO includes a genuine reverse-mode automatic-differentiation engine (the `graph_*` functions): build a computation graph from `graph_const`/`graph_param`/`graph_add`/`graph_mul`/etc., forward-evaluate it with `graph_forward`, and get every parameter's gradient in one `graph_backward` call, no manual calculus required. `graph_dense`/`graph_relu`/`graph_sigmoid`/`graph_mse_loss`/etc. compose that primitive layer into the pieces an actual small feedforward network needs, and `graph_sgd_step`/`graph_momentum_step`/`graph_adam_step` are the parameter-update rules that turn gradients into an actual training loop.

math_notes.linreg_predict: \( \hat{y} = X\beta \) -- matrix-vector multiply of the design matrix (with intercept column, if `linreg_add_intercept` was used) against the fitted coefficient vector.
math_notes.linreg_r_squared: \( R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}} = 1 - \dfrac{\sum_i (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i-\bar{y})^2} \) -- the coefficient of determination: fraction of the target's variance the model explains, 1.0 for a perfect fit, 0.0 for a model no better than always predicting the mean.
math_notes.logreg_predict_proba: \( \hat{p} = \sigma(X\beta) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-X\beta}} \) -- the logistic (sigmoid) function applied to the linear predictor, squashing an unbounded real value into a \( (0,1) \) probability.
math_notes.logreg_predict: Thresholds `logreg_predict_proba`'s output: predicts class 1 if \( \hat{p} \ge \text{threshold} \) (typically 0.5), else class 0.
math_notes.logreg_fit: Fits logistic regression coefficients \( \beta \) by gradient descent minimizing the (binary) cross-entropy loss \( -\sum_i \big[y_i\log\hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{p}_i)\big] \), whose gradient w.r.t. \( \beta \) has the clean closed form \( X^T(\hat{p}-y) \) -- a dedicated gradient-descent loop rather than calling into [vani-optimize](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-optimize) directly, since threading the training data through vani-optimize's fixed `fn` pointer signature would need a ref-capturing closure vāṇी doesn't support (see the README's design note).
math_notes.kmeans_fit: Lloyd's algorithm for k-means clustering: alternates (1) assigning each point to its nearest centroid (by Euclidean distance) and (2) recomputing each centroid as the mean of its assigned points, until assignments stop changing or `max_iter` is reached -- converges to a LOCAL optimum of the within-cluster sum of squares (`kmeans_inertia`), not necessarily the global one, which is why random initialization and multiple restarts matter in practice.
math_notes.kmeans_inertia: \( \sum_i \lVert x_i - c_{a_i} \rVert^2 \) -- the within-cluster sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned centroid, the objective k-means implicitly minimizes; lower is tighter clusters, useful for comparing different \( k \) or different random initializations of the same \( k \).
math_notes.mse: \( \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \) -- mean squared error, the standard regression-error metric.
math_notes.accuracy: \( \dfrac{\text{correct predictions}}{\text{total predictions}} \) -- fraction of labels predicted correctly, for binary \( \{0,1\} \) labels.
math_notes.precision: \( \dfrac{TP}{TP+FP} \) -- of everything predicted positive, what fraction actually was; returns 0.0 (with a documented caveat) when there are no predicted positives at all, matching scikit-learn's convention.
math_notes.recall: \( \dfrac{TP}{TP+FN} \) -- of everything actually positive, what fraction got predicted as such; returns 0.0 when there are no actual positives.
math_notes.f1_score: \( 2 \cdot \dfrac{\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}} \) -- the harmonic mean of precision and recall, penalizing a model that's lopsided toward one at the expense of the other more than a plain average would; returns 0.0 if both are 0.
math_notes.standardize_fit: Computes each feature's mean \( \mu_j \) and standard deviation \( \sigma_j \) across the training data -- the parameters `standardize_apply` uses for z-score standardization \( x' = (x-\mu)/\sigma \).
math_notes.standardize_apply: \( x'_{ij} = \dfrac{x_{ij} - \mu_j}{\sigma_j} \) -- z-score standardization using the `StandardScaler`'s fitted mean/std, giving each feature zero mean and unit variance; apply the SAME fitted scaler to both training and test data (never re-fit on the test set) to avoid leaking test-set statistics into the model.
math_notes.normalize_fit: Computes each feature's min and max across the training data -- the parameters `normalize_apply` uses for min-max scaling.
math_notes.normalize_apply: \( x'_{ij} = \dfrac{x_{ij} - \min_j}{\max_j - \min_j} \) -- min-max scaling into \( [0,1] \) using the `MinMaxScaler`'s fitted range; same train/test-fitting discipline as `standardize_apply`.
math_notes.graph_add: Adds an `Add` node to the computation graph representing \( a+b \) -- pure graph construction; `graph_forward` computes the actual value, `graph_backward` computes \( \partial(\cdot)/\partial a = 1,\ \partial(\cdot)/\partial b = 1 \) when propagating gradients through it.
math_notes.graph_mul: Adds a `Mul` node representing \( a \times b \) -- backward pass applies the product rule, \( \partial(ab)/\partial a = b,\ \partial(ab)/\partial b = a \).
math_notes.graph_div: Adds a `Div` node representing \( a/b \) -- backward pass applies the quotient rule.
math_notes.graph_forward: Evaluates every node in the arena in index order (append-only construction guarantees a node's children always have lower indices, so this single forward pass is already topologically sorted -- no separate topo-sort needed), producing the value each node evaluates to.
math_notes.graph_backward: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation: seeds the root node's gradient to 1, then walks the arena in REVERSE index order, at each node pushing its local derivative contribution back onto its children's accumulated gradients (the chain rule, applied automatically rather than by hand) -- descending index order guarantees every consumer of a node has already contributed its share before that node's own gradient is read as final, the same topological guarantee `graph_forward` exploits in the opposite direction. Returns the gradient of the root with respect to every node in the graph, including every `graph_param` leaf.
math_notes.graph_relu: \( \operatorname{ReLU}(a) = \max(0,a) \), with derivative \( 1 \) for \( a>0 \) and \( 0 \) for \( a<0 \) (subgradient convention at exactly 0) used during `graph_backward`.
math_notes.graph_sigmoid: \( \sigma(a) = 1/(1+e^{-a}) \), with derivative \( \sigma(a)(1-\sigma(a)) \) used during `graph_backward` -- the same sigmoid `logreg_predict_proba` uses directly on real values, here as a differentiable graph node instead.
math_notes.graph_dense: Builds a fully-connected ("dense"/"linear") layer's computation as graph nodes: \( \sum_i w_i x_i + b \) -- a dot product of `inputs` against `weights` (via repeated `graph_mul`/`graph_add`) plus a bias term, all as differentiable graph nodes so `graph_backward` can compute gradients w.r.t. every weight and the bias.
math_notes.graph_mse_loss: Builds \( \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i (\text{pred}_i - \text{target}_i)^2 \) as graph nodes -- the differentiable-graph version of the plain numeric `mse` function above, so its gradient w.r.t. every upstream parameter is available via `graph_backward`.
math_notes.graph_binary_cross_entropy_loss: Builds the binary cross-entropy loss \( -\sum_i\big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big] \) as graph nodes, given prediction nodes (typically the output of `graph_sigmoid`) and target values -- the differentiable-graph version of the loss `logreg_fit`'s hand-written gradient descent minimizes directly.
math_notes.graph_sgd_step: Plain (stateless) gradient descent parameter update: \( \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \, g \) for each parameter \( \theta \) with gradient \( g \) and learning rate \( \eta \).
math_notes.graph_momentum_step: SGD with momentum: \( v \leftarrow \beta v + g \), \( \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta v \) -- accumulates a running velocity \( v \) across steps (weighted by \( \beta \)) instead of using the raw gradient directly, smoothing out oscillation and accelerating progress along consistent gradient directions.
math_notes.graph_adam_step: The Adam optimizer update: maintains a first-moment estimate \( m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1)g \) and second-moment estimate \( v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2)g^2 \), bias-corrects both (\( \hat{m}=m/(1-\beta_1^t) \), \( \hat{v}=v/(1-\beta_2^t) \)) to counteract their zero initialization, then updates \( \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon) \) -- effectively a per-parameter adaptive learning rate, the \( \epsilon \) purely to avoid division by zero.
